data.title: 3 Technology ETFs That Can Deliver 25%+ Gains
data.description:
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT), and Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC) are three technology exchange-traded funds (ETFs) with more than 25% upside potential, according to Wall Street analysts’ average price targets for their holdings.

Technology stocks have been volatile due to concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade and macro pressures. Leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) also affected investor sentiment. However, AI and tech stocks rallied on Monday, as Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.

Despite the ongoing volatility, investors remain interested in capitalizing on the long-term growth potential of tech companies in areas such as AI, cloud computing, quantum computing, semiconductors, and cybersecurity. Tech ETFs help investors gain diversified exposure to attractive stocks while mitigating company-specific risks.

VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH)

The SMH ETF tracks the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor 25 Index and includes stocks of companies involved in semiconductor production and equipment. It is suitable for investors who want to capitalize on the strong growth opportunities of semiconductor companies, which are seeing robust demand from the ongoing AI wave.

According to TipRanks’ unique ETF analyst consensus, determined based on a weighted average of analyst ratings on its holdings, SMH scores a Strong Buy rating. The average price target of $623.04 for the SMH ETF implies 35.4% upside potential.

Currently, the top three holdings of the SMH ETF are Nvidia (NVDA), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM), and Broadcom (AVGO). Overall, SMH has about $59.2 billion in assets under management (AUM).

Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT)

The VGT ETF tracks the MSCI U.S. IMI 25/50 Information Technology Index and comprises stocks of companies in the electronics and computer industries or that manufacture products based on the latest applied science.

Based on a weighted average of analyst ratings on its holdings, VGT earns a Strong Buy rating. The average price target of $135.43 for the VGT ETF implies about 27.3% upside potential.

Currently, the top three holdings of the VGT ETF are Apple (AAPL), Nvidia, and Microsoft (MSFT). Overall, VGT has about $131.3 billion in AUM, way higher than the other two technology ETFs discussed here.

Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC)

The FTEC ETF tracks the MSCI USA IMI Information Technology Index and is suitable for investors seeking exposure to rapid advancements and growth in the technology sector. It includes tech giants and innovative companies across sub-sectors such as software, hardware, semiconductors, and IT services. 

Based on a weighted average of analyst ratings on its holdings, FTEC earns a Moderate Buy rating. The average price target of $318.53 for the FTEC ETF implies about 25.4% upside potential.

The top three holdings of the FTEC ETF are Apple, Nvidia, and Microsoft. FTEC ETF has about $19 billion in AUM.

data.title: Nebius vs. Applied Digital: Which AI Stock Is a Better Buy After Jensen Huang’s Dramatic Return?
data.description:
Nebius (NASDAQ:NBIS) and Applied Digital (NASDAQ:APLD) are getting a second chance on Wall Street, with shares of both AI infrastructure companies soaring more than 20% on Monday. Jensen Huang’s surprise return to Nvidia has breathed new life into a sector that had spent weeks watching its market value evaporate. For investors who endured the selling, Monday’s rally offers a welcome reversal after a turbulent November.

The turnaround began when Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) revealed that its board had unanimously approved Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, just 11 days after his unexpected departure. The decision followed conversations with Huang and consultations involving senior U.S. government officials, which convinced directors that his reinstatement would not threaten national security. Nvidia stock responded with a massive rally of more than 30%.

For neocloud investors, Huang’s comeback could prove especially important given Nvidia’s extensive financial relationships with infrastructure providers. His departure raised concerns about potential disruptions to expansion plans, future processor availability, and the industry’s long-term direction. With that uncertainty easing, Wall Street can once again focus on customer demand, construction progress, and profitability.

Nebius: Nvidia’s $2 Billion Investment Faces Its Biggest Test

Nebius has a valuable advantage over many competitors, considering Nvidia invested $2 billion in the company earlier this year to support its global expansion. The partnership includes plans to deploy more than five gigawatts of computing capacity by 2030, potentially strengthening the cloud provider’s position among hyperscale customers.

However, recent financial results revealed that turning those plans into revenue remains challenging. On November 12, Nebius reported third-quarter sales of $980.8 million, exceeding analysts’ expectations of $907.2 million, while posting a narrower loss of $0.13 per share. Construction delays nevertheless prompted the company to lower its annual revenue forecast toward the bottom of its previous $3 billion to $3.4 billion range.

Looking further ahead, Nebius anticipates generating between $12 billion and $13 billion in 2027 revenue, representing tremendous growth from current levels. Achieving those targets will require massive investment, with projected capital expenditures reaching $40 billion to $45 billion next year. Investors will therefore want evidence that delayed facilities are opening on schedule without creating additional financing headaches.

Applied Digital: A $41 Billion Backlog Changes the Picture

Applied Digital has another reason for Monday’s explosive rally beyond Huang’s reinstatement, having announced a lucrative agreement with a leading hyperscaler. The company secured an 18-year lease covering 150 megawatts of computing capacity, worth $5.4 billion throughout its initial term.

That contract brings total committed leasing revenue above $41 billion, potentially approaching $100 billion should customers exercise every available renewal option. Furthermore, investment-grade clients now account for about 75% of those contracted payments, providing greater visibility into future income.

Unlike Nebius, which supplies customers with access to advanced processors, Applied Digital primarily develops specialized facilities leased to large tech operators. Its expanding portfolio now exceeds 1.6 gigawatts of contracted critical IT capacity, demonstrating the appetite for purpose-built infrastructure.

However, investors shouldn’t overlook the financial commitments required to complete these projects. Applied Digital plans to support construction through existing equity resources, its $5 billion partnership with Macquarie, and additional project financing. The latest contracted capacity isn’t expected to begin delivery until the first half of 2028, making construction milestones especially important.

Which AI Stock Offers the Better Opportunity?

Both companies stand to benefit from Huang’s reinstatement, although their paths toward long-term returns involve different financial considerations. Nebius offers greater exposure to cloud computing revenue growth, supported by Nvidia’s investment and aggressive expansion targets.

Applied Digital, meanwhile, provides an appealing alternative through long-duration contracts that could generate recurring income for decades. Its latest hyperscaler agreement also expands its contracted revenue base while improving the visibility of future cash flows.

Wall Street’s numbers ultimately give Applied Digital the edge, with its Strong Buy consensus and projected 238% return surpassing Nebius’s Moderate Buy rating and 163% potential gain. While neither forecast guarantees future performance, analysts currently see a bigger opportunity in APLD, making it the more compelling choice for investors willing to tolerate the risks associated with large-scale infrastructure development. data.title: ‘Absurd,’ Says Investor About Sandisk Stock
data.description:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) spent just one session trading on its new share count before Nvidia threw it a lifeline. The flash memory maker is rallying on Monday after Nvidia’s board brought back Jensen Huang as CEO, less than two weeks after he resigned. The news has lifted the whole chip group, and memory stocks are among the biggest gainers.

The bounce comes after a rough start to the post-split era. Sandisk fell 16% on Friday, its first day after the 8-for-1 split, as research firm TrendForce forecast that NAND flash contract prices would start falling in early 2027. The stock is up around 15% as of writing, though that still leaves it roughly 69% below its split-adjusted record close from June 25.

Investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to The Motley Fool, sees the split as a sideshow and the business as the main event. A split changes how a stock is sliced, not what it’s worth, and with most brokerages offering fractional shares, a four-figure price tag was never much of a barrier. The practical benefit for Sandisk is that a lower share price makes it easier to give stock to employees. What a split says matters more to Drury: a company rarely needs one unless its shares have climbed a long way, which usually means the business has been delivering.

And it’s certainly true that Sandisk’s business has been delivering. AI data centers are taking every memory chip the industry can make, which leaves buyers bidding for limited supply. That has let Sandisk raise prices while its own costs have barely moved. In the fiscal first quarter (September quarter), cost of revenue was roughly flat year over year even as revenue nearly quintupled. Net profit margin hit about 73%, a level Drury calls “absurd.”

Not everyone is happy about it. Drury notes that people buying phones, laptops and storage drives are paying far more than they did a couple of years ago, and hyperscalers are also paying up to lock in memory for their data centers.

Still, Drury notes memory makers have always had booms and busts, and for much of their history they had more capacity than they could use. The AI demand surge caught the industry short, and Sandisk, like its peers, plans to expand. The danger is building too much and being left with idle factories once AI spending cools. Nevertheless, with that spending expected to run for years to come, Drury thinks some added capacity is justified, and he doubts the shortage will ease soon.

That brings him to valuation. Sandisk trades at just over three times forward earnings, a multiple that tells you investors expect today’s profits to fade quickly. Drury believes that view clashes with what the biggest AI companies have said about their plans. “I think it’s more likely than not that the market is misvaluing Sandisk’s stock, and today it represents an excellent buying opportunity,” Drury summed up. “I think that Sandisk has a ton of potential, and with it being an important component supplier for the AI build-out, the stock is well worth buying.” (To watch Drury’s track record, click here)

Most Street analysts are thinking along the same lines. Based on 11 Buys and 3 Holds, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 192%, given the average price target lands at $266.29. (See SNDK stock forecast)

data.title: Stock Price Forecast: Goldman Sachs Sizes Up Nvidia Stock After Jensen Huang’s Comeback
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is staging an incredible comeback on Monday, with shares of the AI chip giant skyrocketing 31% following the unexpected return of Jensen Huang as CEO. The rally comes after weeks of devastating losses, as investors struggled to imagine the company’s future without its legendary founder. Now, Huang is back, and Wall Street is celebrating his return in spectacular fashion.

The reversal came just 11 days after Huang resigned amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including an alleged relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board unanimously approved his reinstatement following discussions with the executive and input from senior U.S. government officials, concluding that his return posed no national security risk.

But after such an explosive rally, how much higher can Nvidia stock climb? Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider has weighed in on Huang’s comeback, offering an encouraging outlook while warning that several obstacles could still stand in the way.

Goldman Sachs Sees More Upside for Nvidia Stock

Schneider believes Huang’s reinstatement is an important development for Nvidia, particularly given the founder’s influence over the company’s direction and relationships throughout the tech industry.

“We believe Mr. Huang’s vision, reach, and external convening power have been important to both Nvidia and the broader AI ecosystem,” the analyst wrote.

Bringing back the man who transformed Nvidia into an AI powerhouse could help restore confidence among customers and strategic partners, according to Schneider. The analyst also expects the company to maintain its established corporate identity and deliver upcoming products according to its existing schedule.

However, the Goldman Sachs analyst isn’t convinced that everything will immediately return to normal. Schneider remains uncertain whether Nvidia can continue orchestrating enormous financing arrangements involving multiple tech companies and investors at the same pace as before.

Legal complications present another concern. The Justice Department is examining potential export-control violations involving Nvidia customers, while reports have pointed to an SEC investigation into the company’s previous disclosures.

“We believe these investigations are likely to serve as an overhang on the stock until they are resolved,” Schneider cautioned.

Nevertheless, Schneider remains bullish on Nvidia’s prospects, maintaining his Buy rating on the stock alongside a $220 price target, which implies about 32% upside from current levels. The analyst expects investors to assign a higher valuation to Nvidia following Huang’s return, although ongoing government investigations could limit how far the shares climb.

What Does the Rest of Wall Street Think About NVDA Stock?

Turning to the rest of Wall Street, Nvidia currently carries a Moderate Buy consensus rating, based on 31 Buys, 12 Holds, and just one Sell issued over the past three months. The average 12-month NVDA price target stands at $231.92, implying ~39% upside from current levels. Analyst forecasts range from a low of $130 to a high of $350. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: ‘Already Paid,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
For much of the past year, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) has traded less like a software company and more like a running vote on whether the AI building boom can pay for itself. After a brutal week, the vote swung sharply the other way on Monday. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and AI stocks that had been dumped last week came roaring back. Oracle also had news of its own: right after Friday’s close, it posted on X that it already has all the funding it needs for its OpenAI contract.

The stock is up around 13%, bouncing off a 52-week low. That said, even after the rebound, it is still about 65% below its record close from September 2025.

Investor Nicholas Thomas Lowry thinks the market has been punishing Oracle for a problem it has already dealt with. The spending is enormous, with capex guided at $90 billion to $95 billion this fiscal year. But in the investor’s view, the real fear was open-ended dilution and borrowing, with no one able to say how much more Oracle would have to raise.

That question got an answer at the Oct. 28 Investor Day, when Oracle limited new capital-market funding through fiscal 2030 to $20 billion, not counting refinancing. On Nov. 2, it priced the whole amount, about $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds. If Oracle sticks to that pledge, Lowry notes, the fundraising for this cycle is over.

The business, meanwhile, is moving fast. Cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 121% year over year to $7.4 billion in fiscal Q1, and remaining performance obligations hit $664 billion. Lowry is more cautious about the AI agents inside Oracle’s applications. SaaS revenue rose just 10%, and he wants to see that usage turn into revenue first.

He also likes that the plan comes with dates. Capex peaks in fiscal 2027 and 2028, free cash flow is expected to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028, and Oracle targets more than $30 billion of it in fiscal 2029.

The stock trades at about 12 times next-12-months consensus earnings and 9 times fiscal 2028’s EPS estimate of $11.06, versus a five-year average forward P/E near 21 times. Lowry doesn’t expect a full return to that level, since the debt load justifies a lower multiple.

As far as risks go, they are not to be sniffed at. Debt stood at about $125 billion at the end of August, before the new bonds. Another $288 billion of signed data center leases that haven’t started yet sits outside the $20 billion cap. S&P rates Oracle BBB-, one notch above junk, and has estimated that OpenAI makes up about half the backlog. The ChatGPT maker reportedly raised only half of the $30 billion it first sought in its latest round. Lowry is watching two warning signs in particular: Oracle going back to the markets for new money and a cut to junk.

Still, he argues that a heavy spender is usually cheapest while its investments look like they may never pay off. With the money raised and a payback timeline on the table, the investor thinks the low multiple more than makes up for the risk.

Accordingly, Lowry rates Oracle stock a Buy. (To watch Lowry’s track record, click here)

Most on the Street agree. Based on a mix of 28 Buys, 4 Holds, and 1 Sell, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating. At $241.83, the average price target implies shares will gain 112% in the months ahead. (See ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: SanDisk Stock (SNDK) Has More Protection Against a Memory Downturn Than You Think
data.description:
SanDisk (SNDK) stock has more protection against a memory downturn than its steep sell-off suggests, thanks to its growing base of long-term deals. The flash memory (NAND) maker’s stock is down 70% from its June peak, although still up 167% year-to-date. The cycle is mature, but I see no clear signal of its end yet, and when it comes, the deals should soften the downturn. That’s why such a deep sell-off seems unjustified to me.

I follow memory stocks closely, and I’m not suggesting SanDisk is without risks. While the market still prices it like a classic boom-and-bust memory stock, it doesn’t change my view. SanDisk is now one of the fastest-growing companies I follow, and much of its future business is already under contract. Thereby, my rating on SNDK stock is a Buy.

SanDisk’s Cycle Is Mature, but It Isn’t Over

SanDisk’s revenue keeps growing, and management’s guidance for Q2 FY27 implies year-over-year growth above 300%. Still, history calls for caution: from 2002 to 2015, before Western Digital (WDC) bought the old SanDisk, revenue growth periods lasted two to six years, almost four on average, while each decline lasted just one.

Since its Fiscal 2023 low, SanDisk has grown revenue three years in a row, although only the last year was strong, and Fiscal 2027 looks set to be the fourth. The market’s reaction does not surprise me. However, I believe it is overdone.

The operating margin was about 80% in Q1 FY27, the highest in the company’s history. Such a margin can be a trap, because in previous cycles, the highest margins preceded a drop in revenue. At the old SanDisk, between 2002 and 2015, the drop came after another year or two of growth; in the last two cycles at Micron (MU), it came the very next year.

To me, a record margin mainly reflects strong artificial intelligence (AI) demand alongside limited supply, as management expects memory sales in bits to grow only by a mid-teens percentage in Fiscal 2027.

NBM Contracts Cushion SanDisk Against Memory Swings

Under New Business Model (NBM) agreements, customers commit to years of purchases at or above minimum prices and provide financial guarantees. Agreements with eight customers are worth at least $93.9 billion in total at floor prices. Even if the broader market weakens, that contracted portion of sales carries a price floor, provided customers honor their terms.

Previous cycles had no such protection. The old SanDisk sold mainly through purchase orders, and its stock could fall more than 90%, as in 2008 from its all-time high. Even in the last trough, in Fiscal 2023, there were no NBM deals. In my view, the sell-off ignores this change.

Yet these agreements come at a cost and haven’t been tested in a real downturn. Besides floor prices, they include a ceiling, so in a severe shortage, SanDisk gives up some profit. They also tie it to fewer, larger customers, who may challenge them if prices fall sharply.

Chinese competition is also growing, as Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) is already a top-three NAND producer by shipments and plans more factories, which could lower prices. For now, however, YMTC sells more memory for consumer electronics than for data centers. ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), known mainly for dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), also wants to enter NAND, but Reuters says it is unclear when mass production could start.

AI Fears Are Hitting SanDisk Too

SanDisk supplies memory to data centers, so fears about AI companies’ whole business model add to worries about cyclicality. When the market worries about the biggest player, Nvidia (NVDA), memory suppliers fall as well. This pattern was clear on November 20, when SanDisk fell even more than Nvidia.

These worries are understandable, especially as NAND prices are starting to fall. According to research firm TrendForce, spot prices recently dropped more than 20%, and from early 2027, oversupply should push contract prices down, too.

What Would Really Signal the Cycle’s End?

For me, the signal will come when the largest customers start cutting data center spending, because Datacenter is SanDisk’s fastest-growing end market. Slower growth alone isn’t enough, and neither are lower prices, because NBM deals protect part of sales.

TrendForce already gives a first warning, as Chinese cloud companies have cut orders for 2027. However, U.S. providers raised their demand forecasts, and UBS (UBS) estimates that hyperscalers, the largest data center operators, will increase capital spending by 69% in 2027.

Wall Street consensus estimates for 2028 point to slower spending growth, from 3% at Amazon (AMZN) to 12% at Meta (META). SanDisk may feel it, but NBM deals cover about two-thirds of its Fiscal 2028 shipments, so a slowdown should hit it less than before.

A Dollar of SanDisk’s Earnings Now Costs Much Less

The forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio shows how much investors pay for each dollar of adjusted earnings expected over the next 12 months. For SNDK, it is about 2.6x, versus a quarter-end median of about 14x since SanDisk’s 2025 spin-off. Such a low level suggests the market doesn’t believe these earnings will last. I think that discount is too steep, given that NBM price floors and disciplined supply should help support earnings even if spot prices cool, with analysts still expecting adjusted earnings per share (EPS) to roughly quadruple between Fiscal 2026 and 2028.

Free cash flow is high, too. It reached $17.36 billion over the last 12 months, partly from customer prepayments. S&P Global Ratings (SPGI) expects more than $23 billion in Fiscal 2027, though that October forecast predates TrendForce’s warning. It also expects SanDisk’s strong balance sheet, with all funded debt repaid, to help it withstand a downturn.

What Do Analysts Expect from SanDisk?

On TipRanks, SanDisk has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 11 Buys, three Holds, and zero Sells assigned in the last three months. At $266.29, the average SanDisk price target implies about 187% upside potential.

Evercore ISI (EVR) analyst Amit Daryanani argues that long-term agreements are among the factors making NAND more stable than in prior cycles and that investors may be underappreciating this change.

Conclusion

SanDisk remains cyclical, but NBM deals should soften the next downturn, and in my view, today’s price doesn’t reflect that. I understand the concerns about Chinese suppliers and AI spending, but they don’t justify such a sell-off, and I believe the market marked SanDisk down too quickly. I’ll change my mind if customers start pushing back on these agreements, since that is the main reason SanDisk is less cyclical than it looks.
data.author: Karol Kowalczyk

data.title: 3 Best Vanguard ETFs for Beginners With 20%+ Upside
data.description:
ETFs are one of the easiest ways to build long-term wealth. For new investors, low-cost Vanguard ETFs offer broad market exposure and steady growth potential over time. Using TipRanks’ Vanguard ETFs tool, we highlight 3 of the best Vanguard ETFs for beginners: the Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI), the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO), and the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (VYM).

According to TipRanks’ unique ETF Analyst Consensus, which is based on a weighted average of analyst ratings for each ETF’s holdings, VOO, VTI and VYM are rated Moderate Buys. Based on analysts’ price targets, VTI offers the highest upside of over 29%, followed by VOO at 28% and VYM at 21%.

Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI)

The Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) gives investors broad exposure to the entire U.S. stock market. The fund holds companies across large-, mid-, and small-cap stocks, making it a core building block for long-term portfolios. VTI is considered a safe option for long-term investors because it holds thousands of U.S. stocks, spreading risk across the entire market. The fund has an expense ratio of 0.03%.

Currently, VTI holds 3,48 stocks with total assets worth $658.64 billion. Its top 3 holdings are Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Microsoft (MSFT).

Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO)

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF is a popular option for investors looking to gain exposure to large U.S. companies. It tracks the S&P 500 Index (SPX), which is widely seen as a key measure of the overall U.S. stock market and the broader economy.

In terms of holdings, the VOO ETF is heavily weighted toward technology but also includes major exposure to financials, healthcare, consumer, and industrial stocks, giving investors broad, large-cap diversification. VOO holds 506 stocks with total assets worth $1.02 trillion. Its top three holdings are NVDA, AAPL, and MSFT.

Vanguard High Dividend Yield Index ETF (VYM)

The Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF takes a simple approach by investing in a broad mix of companies that pay above-average dividends, making it a well-diversified choice. The fund has a low expense ratio of 0.04%.

Notably, VYM has quietly outperformed the S&P 500 in 2026 so far, benefiting from steady demand for defensive, income-focused stocks. The ETF’s focus on large, dividend-paying companies has helped it hold up better during market volatility, while still delivering competitive returns compared to the broader index.

The ETF owns 593 stocks and manages about $80.01 billion in assets. Among its largest positions are Broadcom (AVGO), JPMorgan Chase (JPM), and Exxon Mobil (XOM).

data.title: Prediction: Where Will Micron Stock Be in One Year After Monday’s Massive Comeback?
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) investors are witnessing an incredible turnaround on Monday, with shares of the memory giant soaring 19% following news that Jensen Huang is returning as Nvidia’s CEO. The rally comes as a welcome relief after weeks of heavy selling wiped billions from Micron’s market value, and Huang’s unexpected comeback may be exactly what investors were waiting for.

The excitement began when Nvidia announced that its board had unanimously approved Huang’s reinstatement, just 11 days after his unexpected resignation. His return followed discussions with senior U.S. government officials, whose input contributed to the board’s conclusion that restoring the legendary founder to his leadership positions would not pose a national security risk. Nvidia shares are surging 34% as of this writing, while Micron has joined the rally amid expectations that demand for advanced memory will remain strong.

Micron plays a crucial role in supplying high-bandwidth memory for Nvidia’s AI processors, making Huang’s return particularly important for the company. His departure had raised fears about potential disruptions to Nvidia’s future expansion plans and the resulting impact on orders for expensive memory components. With the influential executive back at the helm, confidence in the industry’s long-term growth prospects appears to be returning.

Why Micron’s Long-Term Outlook Looks Promising

Micron’s recent struggles have had little to do with disappointing financial performance, as the company continues benefiting from soaring demand for advanced memory products. Its fiscal fourth-quarter revenue reached a record $54.2 billion, while adjusted earnings climbed to $33.42 per share, reflecting favorable pricing conditions. The company also projected first-quarter sales of $61.5 billion, suggesting that its impressive growth trajectory could continue well into 2027.

Yet, those encouraging figures couldn’t prevent a steep sell-off during November, as Nvidia’s leadership crisis and the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections rattled semiconductor investors. Concerns about tighter restrictions on data center construction added to the uncertainty, while growing expectations of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike raised fears that higher borrowing costs could slow AI infrastructure spending and weaken demand for Micron’s advanced memory products.

Looking ahead, Micron has several reasons to remain confident about its prospects, including customer commitments covering more than 75% of planned fiscal 2027 shipments. Meanwhile, its collaboration with Nvidia on customized HBM4E technology could strengthen the company’s position as next-generation processors require greater memory capacity.

Where Does Wall Street See Micron Stock in One Year?

Wall Street appears convinced that Micron has much further to climb, judging by the latest analyst forecasts. The stock currently boasts a Strong Buy consensus rating, supported by 28 Buy recommendations, and just one Hold. That near-unanimous endorsement suggests analysts see strong potential in the memory specialist despite the turbulence investors have experienced recently. The average 12-month price target stands at $1,624.42, implying a potential gain of 130% from current levels. (See MU stock forecast)

Deep Fission is developing small modular reactors designed to operate about one mile underground. The company is still in the development stage, but it has made progress toward its first pilot reactor in Kansas. Year-to-date, FISN stock has fallen 80%.

data.title: ‘No Price Target Hike Yet,’ Says Dan Ives About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
The changes are coming so thick and fast, it’s hard to not get dizzy. In the space of eleven days, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) lost its founder, said it had no plans to bring him back, and then gave him his job back anyway.

On Monday, the board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. Directors said their talks with Huang convinced them he had been honest with them and could still run the company. They added that senior U.S. officials had given input, and the board is now confident his return poses no national security risk. Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after admitting an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. On last week’s earnings call, the chair said there was no intention of reinstating him.

Investors needed no persuading. The shares are up about 32% on Monday, winning back a large part of what they have lost since he left.

So, is the story now done and dusted?

Not quite, says Yorkville Ives’ Dan Ives, an analyst ranked among the top 4% of Street stock experts. Ives is pleased, but he isn’t ready to put a higher value on the comeback yet. As he sees it, the board simply decided that the alternative was worse. That alternative was an Nvidia without its founder at the start of the Rubin product cycle, with a CEO hunt likely running into next year. The board also added new oversight around Huang: a National Security and Export Control Committee made up of independent directors, and a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Harvey Jones stays on as chair, and Colette Kress gives up the interim CEO role and remains CFO.

Ives argues that Huang brings things a stand-in team can’t easily copy. These include his ties with TSMC and the memory suppliers at a time when memory costs dominate the gross margin debate, his long-term product plans with the big cloud customers, his dealmaking across the AI industry, and the speed at which he pushes out new chips. The analyst has said for a while that Nvidia is worth $300 a share with Huang in charge and $225 without him. He also thinks the return calms wider fears about the AI trade, from circular financing to China pulling ahead.

So why keep the lower number? Ives points to what is still unresolved. The independent committee’s probe into the foreign intelligence effort is still going, with Huang cooperating. So are the government inquiries, and the export question remains open. On top of that, a board that went from accepting a resignation to ruling out a return to reversing itself within two weeks now wants investors to treat this call as settled.

In Ives’ view, the $75 gap represents Huang with the governance worries cleared up, not just Huang back at his desk. To close it, he wants to see the committee’s findings, a clean result on the export probe, and a fourth-quarter report where the CEO’s job never comes up.

Demand was never the problem, Ives adds. AI spending keeps orders coming no matter who gives the keynote. “We view today’s news as removing the largest overhang on the stock (and the market) while leaving the ones the board itself named in the release, and we expect to revisit the target as those close,” the 5-star analyst summed up.

For now, Ives keeps an Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating on NVDA shares with a $225 price target, implying roughly 35% upside from current levels. (To watch Ives’ track record, click here)

Elsewhere on the Street, 29 other analysts also remain bullish, while an additional 13 Holds and 1 Sell all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. The forecast calls for 12-month returns of 39%, given the average price target clocks in at $230.57. (See NVDA stock forecast)

Few could have imagined this outcome just six days ago. Nvidia’s board had closed the door on Huang’s return, leaving the company facing an uncertain future without the man who built it. Yet, that door has now swung wide open. Following discussions with Huang and input from senior U.S. government officials, directors unanimously voted to restore him to his former positions, concluding that his return would not pose a national security risk.

Nvidia is also strengthening its oversight, establishing a National Security and Export Control Committee and searching for a chief compliance officer. Meanwhile, Colette Kress has returned to her regular CFO responsibilities, with Harvey Jones remaining board chair.

Where Will Nvidia Stock Be in 12 Months?

Overall, Wall Street still sees room for the stock to climb over the next year. data.title: Anthropic (ANT) Has Plenty of Hype, but Here Are 3 Reasons to Buy the Stock
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) has plenty of hype following its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO), but I believe there are three compelling reasons to buy the stock. The offering raised $93.5 billion, including additional shares sold after the initial offering. Shares were priced at $83, opened at $111.50, and closed at $97.17 on its November 19 debut, up 17%. More than 840 million shares changed hands.

However, the stock reversed course the next day, falling more than 12% by early afternoon on November 20 and giving back nearly all its debut-day gains.

So what now? After all, we’re talking about an artificial intelligence (AI) developer and research lab — best known for its Claude AI assistant — with a fully diluted valuation of around $1.54 trillion at its IPO price.

The valuation is intimidating, as is the reported $104 billion net loss. Yet I see three reasons to buy ANT: explosive growth; customers spending more and more; and a business that’s much healthier than it looks.

That’s why I’m initiating coverage of ANT with a bullish outlook and a Buy rating.

1. Anthropic Is Growing Faster Than Almost Anyone Has Before

Anthropic is growing faster than perhaps any startup in business history. In full-year 2025, Anthropic generated roughly $4.6 billion in revenue. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, revenue reached $17 billion, representing a jaw-dropping 1,127% year-over-year increase. By October, Anthropic’s annualized revenue run rate had climbed to around $81 billion.

To put this into perspective, we’re talking about a company founded in 2021 that’s already generating revenue at a pace comparable to some of the world’s largest technology businesses.

Much of this comes from how Anthropic has positioned Claude, its flagship AI platform, as a core enterprise productivity tool alongside its consumer offerings rather than just as a chatbot. Its capabilities go beyond software development and automated workflows, extending to increasingly sophisticated AI agents. In fact, they’re almost frighteningly sophisticated. Anthropic itself has faced controversy after disclosing incidents in which Claude models accessed real-world systems without authorization during cybersecurity tests.

Of course, growth at this pace won’t last forever. In fact, quarterly revenue growth has already begun to moderate. At the moment, market estimates point to Anthropic generating around $54 billion in revenue in 2026, $127.6 billion in 2027, and $220.54 billion in 2028.

That implies revenue growth slowing to roughly 134% in 2027 and 73% in 2028. Yet here’s the interesting part. Even with growth slowing considerably, Anthropic would still be more than quadrupling its annual revenue in just two years.

We’re talking about a business that could add nearly $93 billion in annual revenue between 2027 and 2028 alone, rather than a small startup growing from a few million dollars in sales. Very few companies in history have operated at that scale, let alone grown this quickly.

2. Claude’s Existing Customers Could Be Its Biggest Growth Driver

Some numbers in Anthropic’s story are arguably even more jaw-dropping than its revenue growth. More specifically, the company’s 900% net revenue retention rate as of September 2026.

For those unfamiliar with the metric, net revenue retention measures how much revenue a company generates from its existing customers compared with an earlier period. It accounts for customers spending more, spending less, or leaving altogether.

Here, a 900% figure means the same group of customers generated 9x as much revenue as a year earlier. That’s truly remarkable.

To me, this points to one of Anthropic’s biggest potential competitive advantages. The more a business integrates Claude into its operations, the harder it becomes to walk away — even with rival models on the market — because replacing a platform woven into core workflows can be costly, disruptive, and require rebuilding internal processes. It may even require rethinking entire processes.

Frankly, I find it hard to imagine a company that has deeply integrated Claude into its daily operations simply deciding to abandon it without a very good reason.

That’s precisely what makes this business so interesting to me. The combination of growing usage and potentially high switching costs could make Claude an exceptionally resilient business over time. Perhaps more importantly, it could also make Anthropic’s revenue increasingly predictable.

3. The $104 Billion Loss Doesn’t Tell the Whole Story

On the uglier side of Anthropic’s IPO, its financial statements look terrifying at first glance.

The company reported a net loss of approximately $104 billion in the first nine months of 2026. That’s an enormous figure, even by the standards of today’s AI industry.

Of course, there’s a catch. According to Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, roughly $94.3 billion of that loss came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and other financial instruments. Much of this reflected the company’s rising valuation.

Sounds contradictory, right? However, as Anthropic became more valuable, so did the equity-linked instruments held by its early investors. Under accounting rules, Anthropic had to recognize that increase as an expense, even though it made no corresponding cash payment.

Because that $94.3 billion charge was purely an accounting adjustment, the headline net loss says very little about how Anthropic’s core operations are performing.

In fact, during the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic generated approximately $6.6 billion in positive operating cash flow, compared with negative $2 billion in the same period in 2025. Its adjusted operating margin also reached 15% in the third quarter, a dramatic improvement from negative 93% a year earlier.

Taken together, these cash flow and margin figures point to meaningful operating leverage, even as Anthropic continues to scale at an extraordinary pace.

Is ANT Stock Worth Buying at This Valuation?

Anthropic is arguably a one-of-a-kind business. That doesn’t mean investors buying shares today are automatically getting a good deal.

Following the November 20 sell-off, Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation fell to approximately $1.54 trillion. Some investment banks involved in the IPO have projected around $53 billion in revenue for 2026, $136 billion in 2027, and $275 billion in 2028.

Based on these estimates, Anthropic would trade at roughly 29.1x projected 2026 revenue, 11.3x 2027 revenue, and just 5.6x 2028 revenue.

That said, those forecasts come with considerable execution risk. Competition from OpenAI, Google (GOOGL), and potentially cheaper open-weight models could become a serious challenge, especially as more alternatives enter the market.

However, if Anthropic comes anywhere close to those expectations, today’s seemingly outrageous valuation could start looking much more reasonable, at least in my view.

Is ANT a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Yes, it’s a Strong Buy. Wall Street coverage of Anthropic began around the IPO, with seven analysts weighing in. Six rated the stock a Buy, while just one went with Hold. The average Anthropic price target stands at $133.33, implying about 50% upside from current prices.

There’s Plenty of Hype, but There’s Substance Too

Anthropic’s IPO arguably comes with a fair amount of hype. Yet it’s hard to dismiss a business growing this fast, with customers spending 9x more than a year ago. Moreover, at just 5.6x projected 2028 sales, assuming those forecasts aren’t too far off, the valuation may not be as crazy as it looks. I’m initiating coverage with a Buy rating.

data.title: AMD’s Blockbuster Q3 Report Is Getting Lost in the Pullback
data.description:
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) delivered a blockbuster Q3 FY2026 report, but the broader pullback in semiconductor stocks is overshadowing its strong results. Revenue reached $13.4 billion, up 45% year-over-year. Growth was driven by record Data Center revenue of $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year on strong demand for EPYC processors and Instinct graphics processing units (GPUs). Looking ahead, management also guided Q4 2026 revenue to about $17 billion.

Despite the recent sector-wide sell-off, I remain bullish on AMD stock and maintain a Buy rating, given its accelerating data center scale and management’s positive outlook for Q4.

For context, AMD designs and sells computer chip processors that power products like servers and personal computers (PCs).

AMD Data Center Revenue 

On the Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CEO Lisa Su stated the company forecasts Data Center segment revenue to be “more than 80% of our total revenue in 2027.” Meanwhile, Q3 revenue was reported at $13.4 billion, up 45% year-over-year, and guidance was set at $17 billion for Q4 FY2026. Adding the first nine months’ revenue of $35 billion to the $17 billion expected in Q4 puts the company on track for roughly $52 billion in FY2026.

Looking ahead, the company expects total revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027, with Data Center revenue making up more than 80% of that. This implies revenue of at least $93.6 billion, including roughly $74.9 billion from data centers. To put that figure in perspective, Nvidia (NVDA) reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue in a single quarter, Q3 FY2027. 

AMD isn’t in the same league as Nvidia, but it is trending upward and comes without all of the risks Nvidia faces going into 2027. The company could capture market share if Nvidia loses momentum due to Jensen Huang‘s departure.

To support management guidance on total revenue, Su mentioned that customers such as Anthropic (ANT) and Meta (META) brought their first Helios racks online this quarter and are already running their latest models on them. The company also pointed to Meta’s Muse, a consumer agentic artificial intelligence (AI) product, as an example of agentic AI growth lifting demand for its EPYC server central processing units (CPUs). This, in turn, supports the expectation that total revenue will grow as enterprise and consumer agentic AI usage increases. Data center and server refresh revenue are the underlying drivers for my bull case on AMD.

Semiconductor Sell-Off Leaves AMD Little Margin for Error

According to Lisa Su, AMD’s “third quarter was the largest and most profitable in our history,” yet the semiconductor industry is seeing a major sell-off since its June 2026 highs. The company’s stock price has fallen nearly 20% over the past five trading days, and the sentiment around semiconductors remains weak. AMD has strong fundamentals, but it has little margin for error in public markets right now.

A consistent theme of risks surrounds the semiconductor and data center trade, and AMD carries them all. On cash flow, it reported free cash flow of $554 million, down from $1.5 billion in Q3 FY2025. CFO Jean Hu attributed this to working capital demands and capex, but I consider it a noteworthy risk if receivables and contracts start outgrowing sales.

Equally important, the market is pricing in the political shift that occurred in the United States. Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections, so investors fear more regulation around data center development in the coming months. For example, Nebius (NBIS) cut its 2026 revenue outlook to the low end of the range due to third-party data center power and construction delays. If similar infrastructure bottlenecks slow customer deployments and leave AMD struggling to clear the inventory it has been building up, that could weigh on AMD’s earnings per share (EPS) and revenue guidance for 2027.

Lastly, Lisa Su specifically acknowledged the memory issue by stating PC sell-through “slowed late in the quarter” due to high memory and component costs. AMD is planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage in 2027.

AMD Has a Proven Track Record for Hitting Expectations

With the primary risks laid out, it’s fair to have concerns. However, AMD has met or beaten TipRanks’ earnings estimates for 16 consecutive quarters since November 1, 2022. Competition and concentration risks affect every major company in this space, but AMD has a proven track record of meeting and exceeding expectations.

AMD trades at a trailing 12-month P/E of 90.73x compared to Nvidia’s P/E of 13.48x. On the surface, that multiple is steep, but with management guiding revenue growth of more than 80% in 2027, I expect it to grow into it over the long term.

AMD ended Q3 with $15.8 billion in cash and short-term investments, up from $10.6 billion at the end of FY2025, with its total principal debt at $7.1 billion. For further context, its debt-to-market cap is around 1% while the semiconductor sector average sits at 2.58%. Backed by a healthy net cash position and a clear path to revenue acceleration, AMD is well positioned to capitalize on its infrastructure investments and the next wave of consumer AI applications.

AMD on Wall Street

Turning to Wall Street, AMD has a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 28 Buy ratings, three Hold ratings, and zero Sell ratings. AMD’s average price target of $652.26 represents 53.69% upside potential over the current price of $424.39 for the next 12 months. 

The Bottom Line

The recent sell-off has AMD down nearly 20% in five trading days, but this is the same company that just reported the largest quarter in its history. Although a trailing P/E of 90.73x leaves little room for error, its balance sheet gives it some room to ride out weaker cash flow and regulatory uncertainty. Based on management’s guidance and the underlying fundamentals, I remain bullish on AMD over the long term, and I think the average analyst price target on Wall Street is within reach.

data.title: AMD vs. Palantir: One AI Stock Is a Buy Now, One Can Wait, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Two of the market’s favorite AI names spent October at record highs and November finding out how quickly that can change. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) makes the chips that run AI models, while Palantir (NASDAQ:PLTR) sells the software that puts those models to work inside companies and governments. Both topped Wall Street’s estimates with their third-quarter earnings reports earlier this month, Palantir on Nov. 2 and AMD a day later. Neither stock held on to the good news for long.

Last week was the roughest stretch yet. AMD tumbled after short seller Hunterbrook published reports on Nov. 19 questioning its China ties and how it finances customers, claims AMD says misrepresent its business. The stock closed Friday about 35% below its Oct. 6 record close. Palantir slid ~6.5% on Friday in a broad AI selloff and now sits more than 30% under its Oct. 9 record close.

Both are rebounding in Monday’s overall bounce, but which one of these AI stalwarts represents a better opportunity right now?

Investor Pythia Research, who ranks among the top 4% of investors on TipRanks, went through both sets of results and came away with a different answer for each stock.

With AMD, the investor is puzzled that the shares are sinking just as the business picks up speed. Revenue rose 45% year over year in the third quarter, data center sales nearly doubled, and management is guiding for roughly $17 billion in the current quarter.

Pythia is focused on two engines. The first is Helios, AMD’s rack-scale AI system, which started shipping in volume last quarter. Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Oracle have all put initial racks into service, and AMD expects its AI accelerator business to outsell its server CPUs for the first time this quarter. The investor sees these deployments as the moment AMD’s long push against Nvidia starts turning into real revenue.

The second engine surprised Pythia more. AMD now expects server revenue to double in 2027, up from an earlier call for growth of at least 70%. The investor links the CPU boost to AI agents, which need plenty of processor power to juggle and carry out their work while GPUs handle inference. OpenAI also picked AMD’s EPYC Turin chips as host CPUs for its first custom accelerator platforms, a sign to Pythia that AMD wins even when customers build their own AI chips.

The investor isn’t ignoring the soft spots. Free cash flow came in at just $554 million as inventory swelled by about $3 billion to nearly $11.5 billion, and that stockpile still has to turn into sales. Helios also carries thinner margins than server chips, and Pythia doesn’t rule out regulatory trouble in China.

Still, with AMD trading at about 24 times 2027 consensus earnings, the investor sees the selloff as another chance to load up, rating the stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Pythia Research’s track record, click here)

Palantir gets plenty of praise, too. Revenue jumped 96% YoY, the adjusted operating margin reached 62%, and U.S. commercial revenue topped U.S. government revenue for the first time. Customers already on the platform are expanding fast, with net dollar retention at 165%. Pythia points to an industrial materials company that went from a pilot worth about $3 million to a $29 million annual contract. The investor also likes what Palantir calls Sovereign AI, which lets businesses use AI on confidential work while keeping control of their own data and models.

The trouble is bookings. Total contract value rose only 6% from a year earlier, and U.S. commercial TCV growth slowed to 11% from 153% in the second quarter, even as U.S. commercial revenue grew 148%. Management blamed shorter Sovereign AI deals, as customers start small and plan to expand later. Pythia accepts that could be the case but worries that revenue is leaning on contracts signed in earlier quarters. The number of U.S. commercial customers, up 29% to 686, is growing far slower than sales.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on Nov. 3, and while Pythia doesn’t expect that to do much damage to the defense business, tougher oversight could slow new contract awards. With the stock still trading at more than 50 times 2027 earnings, the investor wants to see bookings pick up again in the fourth quarter before adding more.

That leaves Pythia with a Hold rating on Palantir.

On the Street, AMD gets a Strong Buy consensus rating, its $652.26 average price target pointing to one-year gains of 54%. PLTR is rated a Moderate Buy, and is expected to deliver returns of 60%, given its average target clocks in at $229.09. (See AMD stock forecast or PLTR stock forecast)

data.title: ‘The Real Story Is Elsewhere,’ Says Investor About Nvidia Stock
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) has spent the past few weeks putting out two kinds of news, and the market only seemed to hear one of them. The business kept reporting better results, while everything around it, from the boardroom to Washington, kept getting worse.

Founder Jensen Huang admitted on Nov. 8 to an affair with a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore customer. U.S. intelligence reportedly suspects her of spying for China. Reports of a second affair, this time with a senior Nvidia executive, came next, and Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12 amid reports that the board was getting ready to remove him. The fiscal third-quarter report on Nov. 17 beat expectations easily but didn’t stop the slide.

On Monday, the story turned again. The board had ruled out a comeback as recently as last week’s earnings call. It has now voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as CEO, a day after President Trump publicly urged it to. The stock is up about 28% in premarket trading, but it’s still roughly a third below its Oct. 6 record close of $239.24.

Even before Monday’s news, Stone Fox Capital (SFC) thought the selling had gotten well ahead of the facts. The quarter was hard to fault. Revenue reached $115.8 billion, about $7 billion more than analysts expected, and guidance for the current quarter of roughly $130 billion also came in above forecasts. Management also lifted its fiscal 2028 outlook and now sees revenue growing about 75% year over year, up from 70%. SFC doesn’t think that’s what a business with fading demand looks like.

The investor doesn’t wave the worries away but argues that most of them have little to do with demand. Washington is looking into Nvidia’s chip sales to China and into Megaspeed. SFC accepts that China revenue could suffer but believes customers elsewhere can absorb the difference. Reuters reported on Friday that the SEC is examining Nvidia’s accounting, but the report gave no details, and the investor sees no grounds for a fire sale until some emerge. SFC also points to Anthropic’s successful market debut last week as a sign that the money behind AI spending is still there.

SFC’s biggest long-term concern was leadership. The investor thought the board was wrong to shut the door on Huang, given how much support he still had among staff and shareholders, and worried that an outside hire would lack his industry relationships. Monday’s decision removes that worry.

That leaves valuation. Even after today’s jump, the stock trades at roughly 10x fiscal 2028 EPS estimates. SFC argues that a multiple this low assumes a downturn that would wipe out AI spending, and the investor doesn’t expect one.

The investigations are now the main risk. The probes into chips that reached China could still turn up something serious, and the SEC’s accounting review hasn’t been explained. Still, SFC sees a business growing at a pace few companies can match, at a price that doesn’t reflect it.

That leaves SFC upgrading NVDA stock from a Buy to a Strong Buy. (To watch Stone Fox Capital’s track record, click here)

On the Street, 30 analysts are also bullish, while an additional 13 Holds and 1 Sell all add up to a Moderate Buy consensus view. At $230.57, the average price target implies shares will gain 44% in the months ahead. (See NVDA stock forecast)

data.title: These 3 AI Tech Stocks Offer 150%+ Upside, According to Analysts
data.description:
Using TipRanks’ Stock Screener Tool, we identified three AI-related tech companies: SanDisk (SNDK), Micron (MU), and Cerebras Systems (CBRS). All three carry Strong Buy consensus ratings from Wall Street analysts, with their average analyst price targets implying at least 150% upside over the next 12 months.

Technology stocks are facing volatility as investors question whether rising AI and data-center spending will generate enough returns to justify the massive investments. Recent earnings have further increased these concerns. Despite these concerns, Wall Street analysts remain optimistic about select technology companies, seeing significant growth opportunities ahead. Here’s a closer look at what is driving their growth potential.

SanDisk (NASDAQ:SNDK)

SanDisk develops NAND flash memory and storage products, including solid-state drives (SSDs), used in data centers, PCs, and consumer devices.

Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani has a Buy rating on SNDK, with a base-case price target of $200 and a bull-case target of $300. He expects strong demand for NAND memory, driven by growing data-storage needs. Daryanani expects NAND products to account for more than 67% of SanDisk’s bit output and over 70% of its free cash flow in the next fiscal year. He also highlighted the company’s plan to return all adjusted free cash flow to shareholders through share buybacks.

On TipRanks, SNDK has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 11 Buys and three Holds. The average SanDisk price target of $266.35 implies 236.1% upside potential.

Micron (NASDAQ:MU)

Micron develops memory and storage products used in smartphones, computers, and AI servers. Its portfolio includes DRAM, NAND flash memory, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and solid-state drives (SSDs).

Recently, Bernstein analyst Mark Li reiterated his Buy rating and $1,300 price target on Micron. His bullish outlook is supported by strong AI data-center demand, tight memory supply, and resilient DRAM pricing. Li forecasts adjusted EPS to increase from $73.78 in 2026 to $173.33 in 2027, implying approximately 135% growth. He believes Micron is well positioned to benefit from the ongoing memory upcycle, although NAND pricing has started to moderate.

On TipRanks, MU has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 28 Buys and one Hold. The average Micron price target of $1,624 implies 173.2% upside potential from current levels.

Cerebras Systems (NASDAQ:CBRS)

Cerebras develops specialized chips and computer systems designed to train and run AI models faster. Its wafer-scale chips combine thousands of computing cores on a single large chip, helping AI systems process information more efficiently.

Recently, Rosenblatt analyst Kevin Cassidy reiterated his Buy rating and $170 price target on Cerebras. Cassidy sees disaggregated inference as a potential growth driver in 2027. The technology reportedly delivers 5x more tokens per megawatt without compromising processing speed, allowing Cerebras to handle more AI workloads using the same amount of power. Its benefits should increase as deployment expands, although delivering computing capacity to OpenAI remains a near-term constraint.

On TipRanks, CBRS has a Strong Buy consensus rating based on eight Buy ratings. The average Cerebras price target of $220.88 implies 167.2% upside potential from current levels.

data.title: ASML Stock’s Sell-Off Looks Excessive Against Its Growth Outlook
data.description:
ASML Holding’s (ASML) stock sell-off looks excessive against its growth outlook, in my view. The lithography equipment manufacturer reported record quarterly sales of €11.7 billion in Q3 2026. During the earnings call, CEO Christophe Fouquet said planned supply for 2027 and 2028 “will not fully meet the demand of our customers.” That is a striking message during a semiconductor sell-off.

While investors are questioning how long the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout can last, ASML’s customers are already asking for more equipment years ahead. Given that disconnect, I think the decline offers an unusually attractive entry point. Thus, my rating on ASML stock is a Buy.

The Sell-Off Overlooks ASML’s Position

The ongoing, brutal market sell-off likely overlooks ASML’s position within semiconductor manufacturing. Investors worry that enormous AI spending could produce disappointing returns. Possible data-center overbuilding and tighter export controls have only added to the pressure. As a result, ASML has been caught squarely in the broader sector retreat, pushing the stock 32% below its 52-week high.

I believe these concerns deserve attention. However, what the market fails to see is that ASML has more protection than many individual chip companies.

ASML is the only manufacturer of Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, which print the finest features on advanced chips. That monopoly insulates the company from the fierce competition among chip designers. Nvidia (NVDA) could lose share to AMD (AMD) or a hyperscaler’s custom processor. However, the manufacturers producing those competing chips would still need ASML’s equipment.

Increasing chip complexity also means more lithography work. The eventual winner among chip designers matters less than continued demand for advanced manufacturing. The most recent Q3 results supported that distinction. Net income reached €5 billion, even if that included a €500 million Mistral AI valuation gain. Gross margin exceeded guidance at 57.5%.

Installed Base Management sales also beat expectations at €3.3 billion, helped by productivity upgrades. Looking further ahead, the demand picture is even stronger. Customer forecasts keep increasing, and planned supply remains insufficient for 2027 and 2028. Some customers are discussing orders for 2029 and 2030. I find those conversations more persuasive than the sector’s current mood.

Growth Has Several Years to Run

Importantly, growth appears to have several years to run if ASML delivers its capacity plans. Q4 guidance calls for €14.2–€15.2 billion of revenue and roughly 57% gross margins. That would be another large sequential increase. Looking ahead to 2027, Low-NA EUV capacity is almost fully covered by orders, despite a planned 30% expansion.

ASML already holds substantial 2028 orders too. It is now investigating increasing 2028 capacity beyond the further 30% previously considered. Demand is rising faster than its earlier manufacturing plans allowed. Customers have also agreed to price increases for critical products. Management expects these to help revenue and margins from 2027, with the full effect starting in 2028.

Underpinning that demand is the industry’s move toward 2nm and smaller chips. AI processors need increasingly advanced logic, while High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) requires sophisticated DRAM manufacturing. More critical layers use EUV as chip designs become harder to produce. Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) immersion equipment remains important elsewhere in the manufacturing process.

Beyond selling brand-new systems, ASML has additional levers for growth. Customers can buy upgrades that let existing machines produce more wafers. I believe that offers ASML additional revenue without waiting for an entirely new fab to open. Also, its advanced-packaging equipment creates another opportunity as manufacturers combine more components within individual products.

Further out on the technology curve, High-NA EUV adds a longer-term reason for optimism. Intel (INTC) already uses it on selected layers of some 18A processors. Other customers are preparing to adopt it as their manufacturing processes advance. These transitions take time, but each adds to ASML’s role in customers’ roadmaps.

Replacing its equipment becomes harder when production processes are developed around it. This is why I see a company helping enable the next generations of chips, with several ways to earn more as the industry advances.

ASML’s Valuation Looks Increasingly Attractive

ASML’s valuation looks increasingly attractive when I look beyond this year. Today, ASML trades at 27.32x 2026 consensus earnings per share (EPS) of $46.35. The multiples fall to 20.05x for 2027, 14.76x for 2028, and 13.13x for 2029. Consensus expects EPS growth of roughly 36% in both 2027 and 2028, making roughly 20x next year’s earnings look reasonable for that outlook.

I believe ASML deserves a premium for its technological lead and long customer relationships. Its installed base also creates substantial service revenue. As a result, projected earnings growth could make today’s price look inexpensive without any valuation rerating.

Buybacks should help boost that per-share growth. ASML’s €12 billion 2026–2028 program includes canceling shares beyond those reserved for employee plans. Management has been executing aggressively: it repurchased €4.1 billion in Q3 alone. The latest disclosed week, November 9–13, added about €443 million. That is roughly 40% above Q3’s average weekly pace.

Purchases were faster still during November 2–6, and I particularly like seeing substantial repurchases during the decline. Lower purchase prices allow the same spending to retire more shares.

The risks still warrant our attention, though. Further China restrictions could reduce equipment sales, and customers might delay fabs. A sharper AI spending slowdown would eventually reach ASML. Increasing manufacturing capacity is costly and difficult, and a handful of major customers heavily influence demand.

The current-year multiple still carries a premium. However, strong order coverage gives ASML time to grow into that valuation. I think the market is allowing too little value for its unusual visibility.

Is ASML Stock a Buy?

Wall Street rates ASML a Strong Buy, with six Buy ratings. The $2,504 average price target implies roughly 98% upside from its current price levels. Thus, analysts see significant upside from here despite the ongoing panic.

Conclusion

ASML’s share price has fallen while customers continue asking for more equipment. Its moat remains intact, and capacity plans point to growth well beyond Q4. Meanwhile, with the stock trading at roughly 20x 2027 earnings and below 15x for 2028, I think the sell-off offers a compelling opportunity. Heavy buybacks only add to that appeal.
